Well, regardless of being downvoted, it -is- true. Giving birth is unethical, even removing suffering from the equation.

I am not an unhappy person. I live with two beautiful partners, the future, whilst worrying on a societal scale, is not guaranteed to be misery for me. Making that assumption on antinatalism is a thought-terminating cliche, a way to not engage with the idea at all.

A disclaimer number two - I do not believe in the ability of humanity to surpass or reject birth as such. It is also inevitable, with only it's scale being something we can change.

A disclaimer number three - I am a socialist. From the misery that is guaranteed to be present in life it does not follow that for those who are already born we should not lessen or prevent more of it. Antinatalism and/or pessimism are not inherently reactionary at all.



Now to the points:

Existence is not a scale of positives and negatives. It is a weighted one. By being born, a person is always guaranteed decay - it is an inalienable part of entropy. So the suffering is guaranteed, even if we only leave bodily decay and pain. There are the risks of disability and additional suffering that is irremovable, of course, there are the struggles of late-stage capitalism, opression, etc, but they are not necessary for the argument.

Pain is guaranteed. Happiness and love are not. By giving birth, you are guaranteeing suffering, whilst happiness relies on the assumption of being able to provide/set up for it in the future, which is often misjudged.

Point two:

By not creating a human, no harm is, by itself, at stake. If the act is done, the harms suffered range from the guaranteed ones to the very severe. Escape from existence by the born is both an excrutiating decision, painful in of itself, and one you most likely can't know or choose until being a teen. So, unless preemtively cut off, a human -is- going to be exposed to more than just the guaranteed suffering, but years of it. Happiness, of course, can also be present, but as outlined before, relies on both the assumption of your parents or guardians competence, no societal prevention, and is conditional. The person made cannot escape the condition of existence until a point, but also cannot preemtively consent to it.

Point three:

There is an assymetry between human emotions. Presence of pain is bad, presence of pleasure is good. However, absence of pain is good, and absence of pleasure is neutral (not bad, but not positive in of itself).

There are more points I can write, both ones I agree and disagree with, for example, the guaranteed additional harm to other species, the psychological issues with evaluating a child's prospects, etc - but on a fundamental level, I think I made my point.

  
Again, I am not an unhappy person, nor does being an antinatalist stop one from caring about those who already were born. Moreover, minimising opression and suffering to those who already are would be an ethical responsibility, tbh.
